stem: Landforms are shaped by the action of various agents of erosion and deposition. The agent responsible for 'fluvial' landforms is:
solution: 'Fluvial' landforms are those shaped by the action of running water — rivers and streams. Running water is the most important and widespread agent of erosion and deposition on the Earth's land surface, and it creates a wide variety of erosional and depositional (fluvial) landforms, such as valleys, waterfalls, meanders, floodplains, and deltas.

stem: A steep drop where a river falls vertically over a hard rock ledge is called a:
solution: A waterfall is formed where a river falls vertically (or nearly so) over a steep drop or ledge — often where the river flows over a band of hard, resistant rock lying over softer rock (the softer rock is eroded away faster, undercutting the hard rock and creating a vertical drop). Waterfalls are erosional fluvial landforms, common in the youthful (upper) course of a river in hilly/mountainous areas. (A very large or high waterfall is a notable feature; over time, waterfalls retreat upstream as the rock is eroded.) Understanding a waterfall (a vertical drop of a river over a rock ledge) is a point. A waterfall is where a river drops vertically over a hard rock ledge.

stem: The large, winding/looping bends that a river develops as it flows across a gentle, flat plain are called:
solution: Meanders are the large, sweeping, winding, looping bends or curves that a river develops as it flows across a gentle, low-gradient plain (in its middle and lower course). As the river swings from side to side, it erodes the outer bank of each bend (where the flow is faster) and deposits material on the inner bank (where the flow is slower), causing the bends to grow more pronounced and to shift over time. Meanders are characteristic of the middle and lower course of a river on a floodplain. (When a meander loop becomes very pronounced and is eventually cut off, it can form an 'ox-bow lake'.) Understanding meanders (the winding bends of a river on a plain) is a point. Meanders are the winding, looping bends of a river on a gentle plain.

stem: A curved/crescent-shaped lake formed when a meander loop of a river is cut off and abandoned is called an:
solution: An ox-bow lake is a curved, crescent- or horseshoe-shaped lake formed when a meander loop of a river becomes so pronounced (looping) that its narrow neck is eventually cut through (during a flood, the river takes a shorter, straighter course across the neck), and the old, abandoned meander loop is left behind as a separate, curved lake (cut off from the main river). The shape of the ox-bow lake reflects the shape of the abandoned meander loop. Ox-bow lakes are depositional/erosional fluvial landforms found on floodplains where rivers meander. Understanding the ox-bow lake (a cut-off meander loop) is a point. An ox-bow lake is a crescent-shaped lake formed from a cut-off meander loop.

stem: The flat, low-lying area of land bordering a river, which is covered with water and sediment when the river floods, is called the:
solution: The floodplain is the flat, low-lying area of land bordering a river (on either side), which is periodically covered with water when the river overflows its banks and floods. When the river floods and then recedes, it deposits a layer of fine sediment (silt) over the floodplain, and over time these repeated deposits build up a flat, fertile plain (floodplains are typically very fertile, due to the deposited silt, and are often important agricultural areas). The floodplain is a depositional fluvial landform, characteristic of the middle and lower course of a river. Understanding the floodplain (the flat, flood-prone, fertile land bordering a river) is a point. A floodplain is the flat, low-lying, flood-prone land bordering a river, built up by deposited sediment.

stem: The fan-shaped or triangular deposit of sediment formed at the mouth of a river where it enters a sea or lake (and drops its load) is called a:
solution: A delta is the fan-shaped, triangular, or arcuate deposit of sediment (silt, sand, and clay) formed at the mouth of a river, where it enters a sea, lake, or other body of standing water. As the river reaches the sea and its flow slows and spreads out, it loses its energy and deposits its load of sediment, building up the delta over time (the river often splitting into several channels — distributaries — across the delta). Deltas are depositional fluvial landforms, and they are often very fertile and densely populated (like the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta, the largest delta in the world). Understanding the delta (the sediment deposit at a river's mouth) is a point. A delta is the fan-shaped sediment deposit formed at a river's mouth where it enters the sea.

stem: The largest delta in the world, formed by the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers, is the:
solution: The largest delta in the world is the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta (also known as the Sundarbans delta, or the Bengal delta), formed by the deposits of the Ganga and Brahmaputra rivers (and their distributaries) where they enter the Bay of Bengal (in India and Bangladesh). This vast delta is home to the Sundarbans (the largest mangrove forest in the world) and is very fertile and densely populated. Understanding that the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the largest delta in the world is a prelims-relevant point. The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta is the largest delta in the world.

stem: The natural embankments/raised banks formed alongside a river channel by the deposition of sediment during floods are called:
solution: Levees (natural levees) are the natural embankments or raised banks that form alongside a river channel (on either side), built up by the deposition of sediment when the river floods. When a river overflows its banks during a flood, the water slows down as it leaves the channel, and it deposits the coarser sediment first, right along the edges of the channel — building up, over repeated floods, raised banks (levees) alongside the river. Levees are depositional fluvial landforms on floodplains. (Levees can also be built artificially to prevent flooding.) Understanding levees (the raised banks along a river, built up by flood deposits) is a point. Levees are the raised banks alongside a river, built up by sediment deposited during floods.

stem: A deep, narrow, steep-sided river valley (often cut in hard rock in the river's upper course) is called a:
solution: A gorge (or, when very large and deep, a canyon) is a deep, narrow, steep-sided (often nearly vertical-walled) river valley, typically cut down into hard rock, especially in the upper (youthful) course of a river where the river is actively cutting down (vertical/downward erosion is dominant). As a river with strong downward-cutting power erodes down into resistant rock (with the valley sides not being widened much), it carves a deep, narrow, steep-sided gorge or canyon. (The Grand Canyon of the Colorado River is a famous example of a canyon.) Gorges and canyons are erosional fluvial landforms of the upper course. Understanding a gorge/canyon (a deep, narrow, steep-sided river valley) is a point. A gorge/canyon is a deep, narrow, steep-sided river valley cut into hard rock.

stem: Glaciers (moving masses of ice) create distinctive glacial landforms. A steep-sided, armchair/bowl-shaped hollow carved by a glacier at the head of a valley (in a mountain) is called a:
solution: A cirque (also called a corrie or cwm) is a steep-sided, armchair- or bowl-shaped hollow or depression carved by glacial erosion at the head (top) of a glacial valley, high in a mountain — where a glacier originates (accumulates and begins to move). The glacier erodes out this rounded, steep-backed hollow through the plucking and abrasion of the rock. (After the glacier melts, a cirque may contain a small lake, called a tarn.) The cirque is a distinctive erosional glacial landform of mountain (alpine) glaciation. Understanding the cirque (the armchair-shaped glacial hollow at a valley head) is a point about glacial landforms. A cirque is a steep-sided, armchair-shaped hollow carved by a glacier at a valley head.

stem: A glaciated valley, deepened and widened by a glacier into a characteristic 'U' shape (with steep sides and a flat/wide floor), is called a:
solution: A U-shaped valley (also called a glacial trough) is a valley that has been eroded, deepened, and widened by a glacier into a characteristic 'U' shape — with steep (often near-vertical) sides and a broad, flat (or rounded) floor. As a glacier flows down a valley (often following a former river valley), it erodes the valley by plucking and abrasion, straightening, deepening, and widening it, transforming the original narrow, V-shaped river valley into a broad, steep-sided, flat-floored U-shaped valley. The U-shaped valley (glacial trough) is one of the most characteristic erosional glacial landforms. (This contrasts with the V-shaped valley cut by a river, which has a narrower, V-shaped cross-section.) Understanding the U-shaped valley (the characteristic glacially-eroded valley) is a point. A U-shaped valley (glacial trough) is a valley deepened and widened by a glacier into a U shape.

stem: The mixed, unsorted rock debris (of all sizes) that is transported and deposited directly by a glacier is called:
solution: Moraine is the mixed, unsorted rock debris — of all sizes, from fine clay to large boulders — that is transported and deposited directly by a glacier (this unsorted glacial deposit is also called 'glacial till'). As a glacier moves, it carries along a load of rock debris (eroded and picked up along the way), and when the ice melts, this debris is dumped/deposited as moraine. There are different types of moraine depending on their position: for example, lateral moraine (along the sides of the glacier), medial moraine (in the middle, where two glaciers join), terminal/end moraine (at the front/end, marking the glacier's furthest extent), and ground moraine (spread beneath the glacier). Moraines are characteristic depositional glacial landforms. Understanding moraine (the unsorted debris deposited by a glacier) is a point. Moraine is the unsorted rock debris deposited directly by a glacier.

stem: Wind (aeolian) action is an important agent of erosion and deposition especially in:
options: Dry, arid regions and deserts (where there is little vegetation and loose, dry material)
solution: Wind (aeolian) action is an important agent of erosion, transportation, and deposition especially in dry, arid regions and deserts. This is because, in arid regions: there is little or no vegetation to hold down the soil and protect it from the wind; the surface material (sand and dust) is loose and dry (not held together by moisture); and strong winds can pick up, transport, and deposit this loose material. So, in deserts and arid areas, the wind is a major agent shaping the landscape (creating aeolian erosional and depositional landforms). (In humid, vegetated regions, by contrast, running water is the dominant agent, and vegetation protects the soil from the wind.) Understanding that wind action is most important in dry, arid regions/deserts is a point. Wind (aeolian) action is most important in dry, arid regions and deserts.

stem: The hills/mounds of sand deposited and shaped by the wind (common in deserts) are called:
solution: Sand dunes are the hills, mounds, or ridges of sand that are deposited, built up, and shaped by the wind — common in deserts (and also in some coastal areas). As the wind transports sand and then deposits it (where its speed drops, or against an obstacle), it builds up dunes, which can take various shapes depending on the wind and sand supply (for example, crescent-shaped 'barchan' dunes, and long linear or 'seif' dunes). Sand dunes are characteristic depositional aeolian (wind) landforms. Understanding sand dunes (the wind-deposited sand hills of deserts) is a point. Sand dunes are the hills of sand deposited and shaped by the wind.

stem: The crescent-shaped sand dunes, with their horns/tips pointing in the direction the wind is blowing (downwind), are called:
solution: Barchans (or barchan dunes) are crescent-shaped (or horseshoe-shaped) sand dunes, with a gentle slope on the windward side (facing the wind) and a steeper slope on the leeward side (sheltered from the wind), and with their two horns or tips pointing downwind (in the direction the wind is blowing). Barchans form where there is a limited sand supply and winds blow consistently from one direction, and they can migrate (move) downwind over time. Barchans are a common and distinctive type of sand dune. (Other dune types include longitudinal/seif dunes — long ridges parallel to the wind — and star dunes.) Understanding the barchan (crescent-shaped dune with horns pointing downwind) is a point. Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes with their horns pointing downwind.

stem: Sea waves and coastal processes create coastal landforms. A steep rock face along a coast, formed by wave erosion, is called a:
solution: A sea cliff is a steep, often near-vertical rock face or slope along a coast, formed by the erosive action of the sea waves. As waves erode the base of the coastal land (by hydraulic action, abrasion, and solution), they undercut it, and the rock above collapses, forming and steadily retreating a steep cliff face (as the sea eats into the land). Sea cliffs are erosional coastal landforms. (Other coastal erosional features include sea caves, arches, and stacks, formed as waves erode the cliffs.) Understanding the sea cliff (the steep coastal rock face formed by wave erosion) is a point. A sea cliff is a steep coastal rock face formed by wave erosion.

stem: An isolated pillar/column of rock standing in the sea near a coast, left behind as the surrounding cliff is eroded (from a former arch that collapsed), is called a:
solution: A sea stack (or simply a stack) is an isolated pillar, column, or tower of rock standing in the sea, just off the coast, left behind as the surrounding rock/cliff is eroded away by the waves. Sea stacks typically form through a sequence of wave erosion: waves erode a cave into a headland; the cave is enlarged and eroded through the headland to form a natural arch; and when the top of the arch eventually collapses, the seaward part is left standing as an isolated stack. Sea stacks are erosional coastal landforms. Understanding the sea stack (the isolated rock pillar left by wave erosion) is a point. A sea stack is an isolated pillar of rock left standing in the sea by wave erosion.

stem: The gently-sloping accumulation of sand and pebbles deposited by waves along a shoreline is called a:
solution: A beach is the gently-sloping accumulation or deposit of loose material — sand, pebbles, shingle, and shells — deposited by the waves along a shoreline (at the edge of the sea). As waves wash material back and forth along the shore, they deposit sand and pebbles, building up the beach. Beaches are depositional coastal landforms, formed by the deposition of material by the waves. Understanding the beach (the depositional accumulation of sand/pebbles along the shore) is a point about coastal landforms. A beach is the gently-sloping deposit of sand and pebbles along a shoreline, formed by wave deposition.

stem: Groundwater is an important agent of erosion and deposition especially in regions of __________ rock (which it dissolves).
solution: Groundwater (underground water) is an important agent of erosion and deposition especially in regions of limestone (and other soluble carbonate rocks). This is because groundwater (which is slightly acidic, containing dissolved carbon dioxide as carbonic acid) can dissolve limestone (by the process of carbonation/solution), creating distinctive underground and surface landforms. In limestone (karst) regions, groundwater dissolves the rock to form caves, caverns, and underground passages (erosional), and the deposition of the dissolved calcium carbonate (as the water drips and evaporates in caves) forms features like stalactites and stalagmites (depositional). Thus, groundwater is especially active as a geomorphic agent in limestone regions (which it dissolves). Understanding that groundwater is most important in limestone (soluble) rock regions is a point. Groundwater is especially active in limestone regions, which it dissolves.

stem: The icicle-like deposits of calcium carbonate that hang down from the roof of a limestone cave are called:
solution: Stalactites are the icicle-like deposits of calcium carbonate that hang down (grow downward) from the roof/ceiling of a limestone cave. They form as water, containing dissolved calcium carbonate (from the dissolved limestone), drips slowly from the cave roof; as each drop hangs and partly evaporates or loses carbon dioxide, it deposits a tiny amount of calcium carbonate, and over long periods these deposits build up into the hanging, icicle-like stalactites. (The corresponding deposits that build up from the floor of the cave — where the drips land — growing upward, are called stalagmites. A tip to remember: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling; stalaGmites grow from the Ground.) Stalactites (and stalagmites) are depositional landforms of limestone caves, formed by groundwater. Understanding stalactites (the hanging cave deposits) is a point. Stalactites are the icicle-like calcium carbonate deposits hanging from a cave roof.

stem: In the youthful (upper) course of a river, the dominant type of erosion is __________, which produces a narrow, steep-sided valley.
solution: In the youthful (upper) course of a river — in the hills or mountains near its source, where the gradient (slope) is steep and the river flows fast — the dominant type of erosion is vertical (downward) erosion: the river cuts down into its bed, deepening its channel. This vertical cutting, without much widening, produces a narrow, deep, steep-sided valley (typically V-shaped, and where the rock is hard, a gorge or canyon). In the later (mature and old) stages, as the gradient lessens, lateral (sideways) erosion and deposition become more important, widening the valley into a floodplain. Understanding that vertical erosion dominates in a river's youthful upper course (producing a narrow, deep valley) is a point. Vertical (downward) erosion dominates in a river's youthful upper course, cutting a narrow, steep-sided valley.

stem: The narrow, steep-sided valley with a cross-section shaped like the letter 'V', typical of a river's upper course, is called a:
solution: A V-shaped valley is a narrow, steep-sided valley with a cross-section shaped like the letter 'V', typical of a river's youthful upper course. It forms because, in the upper course, the river erodes mainly downward (vertical erosion), cutting a deep, narrow channel, while weathering and mass movement on the valley sides give the valley its sloping V-shaped cross-section. This contrasts with the broad, flat-floored, steep-sided U-shaped valley cut by a glacier. Understanding the V-shaped valley (the river-cut valley of the upper course) is a point. A V-shaped valley is the narrow, steep-sided river valley of the upper course.

stem: The fan- or cone-shaped deposit of sediment laid down where a stream flows out from a steep mountain onto a flat plain (and its gradient suddenly decreases) is called an:
solution: An alluvial fan is a fan- or cone-shaped deposit of sediment (alluvium) laid down where a fast stream, carrying a heavy load, flows out from a steep, narrow mountain valley onto a flat plain or a broad valley floor. As the stream leaves the confined, steep mountain course and reaches the flat land, its gradient (slope) suddenly decreases, its velocity drops, and it loses the energy to carry its load — so it deposits the sediment, spreading it out in a fan shape at the mountain foot. Alluvial fans are depositional fluvial landforms found at the base of mountains. Understanding the alluvial fan (the fan-shaped deposit at a mountain foot) is a point. An alluvial fan is the fan-shaped sediment deposit where a stream leaves a mountain for a plain.

stem: A river channel that divides into a network of several small, interlacing channels separated by temporary sediment bars/islands is described as a __________ channel.
solution: A braided channel (braided river) is a river channel that divides into a network of several small, interlacing, or interweaving channels, separated by small, temporary islands or bars of sediment (sand and gravel), giving the appearance of a braid. Braiding occurs where a river carries a large load of sediment (more than it can transport) and has variable flow, so that it deposits the excess sediment as bars within the channel, splitting the flow around them. Braided channels are common where there is abundant sediment, such as on some plains and at glacier fronts. Understanding the braided channel (the multi-channel, sediment-choked river) is a point. A braided channel is a river split into several interlacing channels around sediment bars.

stem: The small lake that occupies a cirque (the armchair-shaped hollow) after the glacier has melted away is called a:
solution: A tarn is a small mountain lake that occupies a cirque (corrie) — the steep-sided, armchair-shaped hollow carved by a glacier at a valley head — after the glacier has melted away. The overdeepened basin of the cirque, once vacated by the ice, fills with water (from rain and snowmelt) to form the small, often circular tarn. Tarns are features of formerly glaciated mountain regions. Understanding the tarn (the small lake in a cirque) is a point about glacial landforms. A tarn is the small lake occupying a cirque after the glacier melts.

stem: The sharp, knife-edged ridge that forms between two adjacent cirques (or glacial valleys) eroding back-to-back is called an:
solution: An arête is a sharp, narrow, knife-edged, jagged ridge that forms between two adjacent cirques (or two glacial valleys) as they erode headward (backward) toward each other, leaving a thin rock wall between them. As glaciers on either side pluck and abrade the rock, the ridge between them is progressively narrowed and sharpened into the steep, knife-edged arête. Arêtes are erosional glacial landforms of high mountains. (Where three or more cirques erode back-to-back around a peak, they can produce a sharp, pyramidal peak or 'horn'.) Understanding the arête (the knife-edged ridge between cirques) is a point. An arête is a sharp, knife-edged ridge between two cirques or glacial valleys.

stem: A sharp, steep-sided, pyramid-shaped mountain peak formed where several cirques erode back-to-back around it (as the Matterhorn) is called a:
solution: A horn (or pyramidal peak) is a sharp, steep-sided, pyramid-shaped mountain peak formed where three or more cirques erode headward (backward) back-to-back around a single summit, cutting into it from several sides until only a sharp, pointed peak remains in the middle. The famous Matterhorn in the Alps is a classic example of a horn. Horns are erosional glacial landforms of high mountains. Understanding the horn (the pyramidal glacial peak) is a point. A horn is a sharp, pyramid-shaped peak formed by cirques eroding back-to-back around it.

stem: A smaller tributary glacial valley that is left 'hanging' high above the main (deeper) glacial valley — often with a waterfall plunging from it — is called a:
solution: A hanging valley is a smaller, tributary glacial valley whose floor lies high above the floor of the main (larger, deeper) glacial valley it joins — left 'hanging' because the smaller tributary glacier eroded less deeply than the larger main-valley glacier. After the ice melts, a stream flowing down the tributary valley often plunges as a waterfall from the hanging valley down into the deeper main valley. Hanging valleys are erosional glacial landforms. Understanding the hanging valley (the tributary valley left high above the main valley) is a point. A hanging valley is a tributary glacial valley left high above the deeper main valley, often with a waterfall.

stem: A long, winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel, deposited by a stream flowing in a tunnel beneath a glacier, is called an:
solution: An esker is a long, narrow, winding (sinuous) ridge of sorted (layered) sand and gravel, deposited by a meltwater stream that flowed in a tunnel within or beneath a glacier. When the glacier melts away, the sediment that had accumulated in the sub-glacial stream channel is left behind as the winding esker ridge. Eskers are depositional glacial (fluvioglacial) landforms. Understanding the esker (the winding ridge of glacial meltwater deposits) is a point. An esker is a winding ridge of sand and gravel deposited by a stream beneath a glacier.

stem: A smooth, elongated, oval hill (shaped like an inverted spoon or half-egg) formed of glacial till, deposited and shaped beneath a moving glacier, is called a:
solution: A drumlin is a smooth, elongated, oval or streamlined hill (shaped like an inverted spoon, or the back of a half-buried egg) formed of glacial till (unsorted debris), deposited and moulded/shaped beneath a moving glacier. Its long axis lies parallel to the direction of ice flow, with the steeper, blunter end facing the direction from which the ice came. Drumlins often occur in groups ('basket of eggs' topography). They are depositional glacial landforms. Understanding the drumlin (the streamlined hill of glacial till) is a point. A drumlin is a smooth, elongated hill of glacial till shaped beneath a moving glacier.

stem: The wind can lower a desert surface by removing loose, dry sand and dust — a process of wind erosion called:
solution: Deflation is the process of wind erosion in which the wind lifts and removes (blows away) loose, dry, fine material — sand, dust, and silt — from a surface, thereby lowering the land surface. In deserts, deflation can scoop out shallow depressions or hollows (called deflation hollows or blowouts) by removing the loose material. (The other main process of wind erosion is abrasion — the sand-blasting wearing-away of rock by wind-driven sand. Wind transport of the finest dust over long distances, and its deposition, forms 'loess'.) Understanding deflation (the wind's removal of loose material) is a point about aeolian processes. Deflation is the wind erosion process of blowing away loose material and lowering the surface.

stem: The wearing away and undercutting of rocks near the ground by wind-driven sand (a sand-blasting action, strongest close to the surface) is the wind-erosion process of:
solution: Abrasion is the wind-erosion process in which wind-driven sand and particles wear away, scour, and polish rocks — a natural sand-blasting action. Because the wind carries most of its sand load close to the ground, abrasion is strongest near the surface, which is why it undercuts rocks near their base (helping to form features like mushroom/pedestal rocks, which are undercut into a narrow stem). Abrasion, together with deflation, shapes many desert (aeolian erosional) landforms. Understanding wind abrasion (the sand-blasting wearing-away of rock) is a point. Wind abrasion is the sand-blasting wearing-away of rock by wind-driven sand, strongest near the ground.

stem: A desert rock with a broad top and a narrow, undercut base (shaped like a mushroom), formed because wind abrasion is strongest near the ground, is called a:
solution: A mushroom rock (also called a pedestal rock or gara) is a desert rock with a broad, wide top and a narrow, undercut base — shaped like a mushroom. It forms because wind abrasion (the sand-blasting action of wind-driven sand) is strongest near the ground (where the wind carries most of its sand), so the lower part of a rock is worn away and undercut faster than the upper part, leaving a narrow stem supporting a broader cap. Mushroom rocks are erosional aeolian (wind) landforms of deserts. Understanding the mushroom rock (the wind-undercut rock) is a point. A mushroom rock is a desert rock with a broad top and narrow undercut base, formed by wind abrasion near the ground.

stem: The deposits of fine, wind-blown, yellowish dust/silt (often carried far from deserts and forming very fertile soils) are called:
solution: Loess is the deposit of fine, wind-blown (aeolian), yellowish dust and silt, which the wind can carry over long distances (far from the deserts or glacial outwash areas where it originates) before depositing it in thick blankets. Loess deposits form very deep, fertile soils and are agriculturally important; extensive loess deposits are found, for example, in northern China (the Loess Plateau). Loess is a depositional aeolian landform/deposit. Understanding loess (the fertile wind-blown dust deposit) is a point. Loess is the fine, wind-blown dust/silt deposit that forms fertile soils.

stem: The sequence by which wave erosion of a coastal headland produces a sea stack is correctly ordered as:
options: Cave → arch → stack (as the arch roof collapses)
solution: The sequence of coastal wave erosion that produces a sea stack is: first, waves erode a hollow into a headland to form a sea cave; then, continued erosion (sometimes cutting right through a narrow headland, or joining two caves) enlarges the cave into a natural arch; and finally, when the roof of the arch is undercut and collapses, the outer, seaward portion is left standing alone as an isolated pillar — a sea stack. (A stack, further eroded and reduced to a low stump, becomes a 'stack stump'.) So the order is cave → arch → stack. Understanding this cave-arch-stack sequence of coastal erosion is a prelims-relevant point. Wave erosion progresses: sea cave → arch → (roof collapses) → stack.

stem: A tunnel-like opening eroded by waves into the base of a sea cliff (often along a line of weakness) is called a:
solution: A sea cave is a hollow, tunnel-like opening or cavity eroded by the waves into the base of a sea cliff or headland, usually along a line of weakness in the rock (such as a joint, fault, or a band of softer rock). Waves concentrate their erosive action (hydraulic action and abrasion) on these weak points, hollowing out the cave. Sea caves are erosional coastal landforms, and they are the first stage in the sequence that can lead to arches and stacks. Understanding the sea cave (the wave-eroded hollow in a cliff base) is a point. A sea cave is a hollow eroded by waves into the base of a sea cliff.

stem: When waves erode a passage right through a narrow coastal headland, leaving a bridge of rock over an opening, the resulting landform is a:
solution: A sea arch is formed when waves erode a passage right through a narrow coastal headland — for example, by enlarging a sea cave until it cuts through to the other side, or by two caves on opposite sides of a headland joining up — leaving an arch or bridge of rock spanning the opening (with the sea passing beneath it). The sea arch is an intermediate stage in coastal erosion: with further erosion, the roof of the arch eventually collapses, leaving the seaward part as an isolated sea stack. Sea arches are erosional coastal landforms. Understanding the sea arch (the rock bridge through a headland) is a point. A sea arch is a rock bridge left where waves erode through a headland.

stem: A long, narrow ridge of sand or shingle, deposited by waves and currents, that is joined to the land at one end and projects out into the sea (or across a bay), is called a:
solution: A spit is a long, narrow ridge or bank of sand or shingle, deposited by the waves and longshore currents, that is attached (joined) to the land at one end and projects out into the sea, often across the mouth of a bay or estuary, with its free (seaward) end frequently curved or hooked. Spits form where longshore drift (the movement of material along a coast by waves) carries material along the shore and deposits it beyond a bend in the coastline. Spits are depositional coastal landforms. (If a spit grows right across a bay, it can form a bar, enclosing a lagoon behind it.) Understanding the spit (the sand ridge projecting from the coast) is a point. A spit is a ridge of sand/shingle attached to land at one end and projecting into the sea.

stem: A shallow body of salt or brackish water separated from the open sea by a sandbar, spit, or barrier is called a:
solution: A lagoon is a shallow body of water (usually salt or brackish) that is separated, or partly cut off, from the open sea by a barrier such as a sandbar, a spit, or a coral reef/barrier island. When a bar or spit grows across the mouth of a bay, it can enclose the water behind it, forming a lagoon. (India's Chilika Lake in Odisha is a well-known coastal lagoon, and Pulicat is another.) Lagoons are associated with depositional coastal landforms (bars/spits). Understanding the lagoon (the water body enclosed behind a coastal bar) is a point. A lagoon is a shallow water body separated from the sea by a bar or spit.

stem: The gently-sloping, rocky platform left at the base of a retreating sea cliff, exposed at low tide, is called a:
solution: A wave-cut platform (or shore platform) is a gently-sloping, flat or nearly-flat, rocky surface left at the base of a sea cliff as the cliff is eroded and retreats landward. As waves undercut and erode the base of the cliff, causing it to collapse and retreat, they leave behind this gently-sloping bench of rock at the foot of the cliff, which is often exposed at low tide. The wave-cut platform is an erosional coastal landform. Understanding the wave-cut platform (the rock bench at a cliff foot) is a point. A wave-cut platform is the gently-sloping rock bench left at the base of a retreating sea cliff.

stem: In a limestone (karst) region, a surface depression or funnel-shaped hollow formed by the dissolving (and sometimes collapse) of the limestone, through which water drains underground, is called a:
solution: A sinkhole (also called a doline) is a surface depression or funnel-/bowl-shaped hollow in a limestone (karst) region, formed by the dissolving (solution) of the limestone by slightly acidic water — and sometimes by the collapse of the roof of an underground cavity/cave below. Surface water often drains down into the ground through sinkholes, disappearing into the underground drainage system of the karst region. Sinkholes are erosional karst (groundwater) landforms. (Many sinkholes can join to form a larger, elongated depression called a 'uvala'.) Understanding the sinkhole/doline (the karst surface depression) is a point. A sinkhole (doline) is a surface depression in limestone formed by dissolving/collapse, draining water underground.

stem: The deposits of calcium carbonate that build up from the FLOOR of a limestone cave (growing upward, where the drips land) are called:
solution: Stalagmites are the deposits of calcium carbonate that build up from the floor of a limestone cave, growing upward, at the spot where the mineral-rich water drips down and lands from the cave roof. As each drop lands and evaporates/loses carbon dioxide, it deposits a little calcium carbonate on the floor, and over long periods these build up into the upward-growing stalagmites. (The corresponding deposits hanging down from the roof are stalactites; a stalagmite and a stalactite growing toward each other may eventually join to form a column/pillar.) A tip: stalaGmites grow from the Ground; stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling. Stalagmites are depositional karst (groundwater) landforms. Understanding stalagmites (the upward-growing cave-floor deposits) is a point. Stalagmites are the calcium carbonate deposits growing upward from a cave floor.

stem: When a stalactite (hanging from the roof) and a stalagmite (rising from the floor) grow toward each other and join, the continuous feature formed is called a:
solution: When a stalactite (growing downward from the cave roof) and a stalagmite (growing upward from the cave floor) grow toward each other and eventually meet and join, they form a continuous pillar or column of calcium carbonate connecting the roof and floor of the limestone cave. Pillars/columns are depositional karst (groundwater) landforms found in limestone caves. Understanding the pillar/column (formed by a joined stalactite and stalagmite) is a point. A pillar (column) forms when a stalactite and a stalagmite join together.

stem: The deep, plunge-pool basins and the circular, pothole-like hollows drilled into a river bed by the swirling action of water armed with pebbles are examples of the river-erosion process of:
solution: Potholes — circular holes or hollows drilled into a river bed — and the deepening of plunge pools (at the foot of waterfalls) are produced mainly by abrasion (also called corrasion): the mechanical wearing-away and grinding of the river bed by the river's load (the sand, pebbles, and boulders it carries). Where the water swirls (in eddies), it spins pebbles round and round in one spot, and these grinding pebbles drill circular potholes into the rock of the river bed. Abrasion by the load is one of the main ways a river erodes its bed (others include hydraulic action and solution). Understanding abrasion/potholes (the river's load grinding out its bed) is a point. Potholes are drilled into a river bed by abrasion — swirling water grinding pebbles into the rock.

stem: A long, deep, steep-sided glaciated valley that has been drowned/flooded by the sea (as along the coasts of Norway) is called a:
solution: A fjord (or fiord) is a long, deep, narrow, steep-sided glaciated valley (glacial trough) that has been drowned or flooded by the sea — that is, a former U-shaped valley cut by a glacier down to (or below) sea level, later invaded by the sea when the ice melted and/or sea level rose. Fjords are characteristic of formerly glaciated mountainous coasts, most famously the coast of Norway (and also found in New Zealand, Chile, and elsewhere). A fjord is a glacial landform modified by the sea. Understanding the fjord (the drowned glacial valley) is a point. A fjord is a deep, steep-sided glaciated valley drowned by the sea.

stem: The broad, gently-sloping plain of sorted sand and gravel, laid down by meltwater streams beyond the front (snout) of a glacier, is called an:
solution: An outwash plain (or sandur) is a broad, gently-sloping plain of sorted (layered) sand and gravel, deposited by the braided meltwater streams that flow out beyond the front (snout/terminus) of a glacier. As the meltwater emerges from the melting glacier carrying sediment, it spreads out and deposits the sorted material in a fan or plain in front of the ice. Outwash plains are depositional glacial (fluvioglacial) landforms, formed beyond the terminal moraine. Understanding the outwash plain (the sorted meltwater deposits beyond a glacier) is a point. An outwash plain is the sorted sand-and-gravel plain deposited by meltwater beyond a glacier's front.

stem: As landforms evolve over a very long period of erosion, an upland region may be worn down almost to a low, gently-undulating, near-level plain; such a nearly-featureless plain of very advanced erosion is called a:
solution: A peneplain (literally 'almost a plain') is a low, gently-undulating, nearly-level plain produced by a very long period of erosion (chiefly by running water), in which an original upland or region of high relief is gradually worn down almost to a featureless plain, close to base level (sea level). The peneplain represents an advanced (old-age) stage in the evolution of a landscape, illustrating how landforms are progressively lowered and reduced over long spans of geological time. (Occasional resistant residual hills, called monadnocks, may rise above the peneplain.) Understanding the peneplain (the near-level plain of advanced erosion) is a point about how landforms evolve over time. A peneplain is a low, nearly-level plain produced by very long-continued erosion of an upland.

stem: The isolated, resistant residual hill (of hard rock) that is left standing above a peneplain or an eroded plain, having survived the general lowering of the land, is called a:
solution: A monadnock (in an arid setting often called an inselberg — 'island mountain') is an isolated hill or knob of hard, resistant rock that stands out prominently above a surrounding eroded plain or peneplain, having resisted and survived the general lowering (wearing-down) of the land around it. Because the rock of the monadnock is more resistant to erosion than its surroundings, it is left behind, standing as a residual upland, while the softer rock around it has been worn away. Monadnocks/inselbergs are residual erosional landforms, illustrating differential erosion (harder rock resists erosion). Understanding the monadnock/inselberg (the residual resistant hill on a plain) is a point. A monadnock (inselberg) is an isolated, resistant residual hill left standing above an eroded plain.

stem: The dry, level, salt-encrusted floor of a desert basin — where a temporary shallow lake forms after rain and then evaporates, leaving salts behind — is called a:
solution: A playa (also called a salt flat, and in some regions a 'salt lake' or 'salina') is the flat, level, often salt-encrusted floor of an enclosed desert basin (a basin of interior/inland drainage, with no outlet to the sea). After occasional heavy rains, water collects in the basin to form a shallow, temporary lake; but in the hot, dry desert climate this water soon evaporates, leaving behind a flat deposit of fine sediment and dissolved salts (a salt crust) on the basin floor. Playas are depositional landforms of arid (desert) basins. Understanding the playa (the salt-encrusted desert basin floor) is a point. A playa is the flat, salt-encrusted floor of a desert basin where a temporary lake evaporates.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Landforms and their Evolution' is that:
options: Landforms never change and appear randomly

The various agents of erosion and deposition (running water, glaciers, wind, groundwater, and sea waves) create a great variety of characteristic erosional and depositional landforms, and landforms evolve/change over time as these processes act on them
Only one agent shapes all landforms
Landforms have no relation to processes
solution: The chapter conveys that the great variety of landforms on the Earth's surface is created and shaped by the various agents of erosion and deposition — running water (rivers), glaciers (ice), wind, groundwater, and sea waves — each of which produces its own characteristic erosional and depositional landforms, and that landforms are not static but evolve and change over time as these geomorphic processes continue to act on them. Each agent creates distinctive landforms: running water (fluvial) creates valleys, waterfalls, gorges, meanders, ox-bow lakes, floodplains, levees, and deltas; glaciers (glacial) create cirques, U-shaped valleys, and moraines; wind (aeolian), especially in deserts, creates features like sand dunes (e.g., barchans); groundwater, especially in limestone (karst) regions, creates caves, sinkholes, stalactites, and stalagmites; and sea waves (coastal) create sea cliffs, caves, arches, stacks, and beaches. These landforms evolve and change over time as the processes of erosion and deposition continue (for example, a river valley evolves from a narrow V-shape in its youthful upper course to a broad floodplain and delta in its old lower course). Thus, the great variety of landforms results from the action of the different agents of erosion and deposition, and landforms are dynamic, evolving features of the ever-changing Earth's surface. Understanding the characteristic landforms created by the different agents (fluvial, glacial, aeolian, karst, and coastal), and how landforms evolve over time, is the central concern of geomorphology and of this chapter, and it completes the picture (begun in the chapter on geomorphic processes) of how the Earth's surface is shaped. The various agents of erosion and deposition create a great variety of characteristic landforms, which evolve over time.
